sections.title: Basic Concept of Figure Analogy
sections.content: In figure analogy, the relationship between A and B must be applied in the same way to C to find D. Step 1: Identify the transformation between A and B. Step 2: Check whether there is rotation, inversion, or shape change. Step 3: Apply the same rule to C. Step 4: The figure that shows the same transformation is the correct answer.

sections.title: Simple Transformations
sections.content: In many questions, figures undergo simple transformations. Step 1: Check whether the shape is flipped or inverted. Step 2: Observe whether the inner and outer shapes have changed. Step 3: Check whether the number of sides in a polygon has increased or decreased. Step 4: Apply the same pattern to the next figure. Example: A triangle may change into a square if one side is added.

sections.title: Figure Classification (Odd One Out)
sections.content: In figure classification, one figure is different from the other four or five figures. Step 1: Carefully observe all the figures. Step 2: Identify a common rule (such as number of lines, shape type, or direction). Step 3: The figure that breaks the rule is the odd one out. Example: If three figures have four lines and one figure has three lines, that figure is the different one.

sections.title: Simple Rotations
sections.content: Rotation means turning a figure around a point. Step 1: Check whether the figure rotates clockwise or anticlockwise. Step 2: Identify the rotation angle such as 90° or 180°. Step 3: Match the direction and orientation. Step 4: Select the correctly rotated figure. Example: If an arrow rotates 90° clockwise, it will point to the right instead of upward.

sections.title: Strategy to Identify Patterns
sections.content: Step 1: Count the sides of the figure. Step 2: Observe lines, dots, or shading. Step 3: Check orientation or rotation. Step 4: Compare symmetry or pattern among the figures.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Confusing rotation with mirror reflection. 2. Not carefully counting the number of lines. 3. Ignoring inner and outer shapes. 4. Assuming a pattern too quickly without checking all figures.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In figure analogy, identifying the transformation rule is essential. In classification, you must find the common rule and identify the figure that breaks it. In rotation-based questions, matching the correct direction and degree of rotation is important.

tricks.title: Compare A and B First
tricks.explanation: In analogy questions, first identify the rule between A and B.
tricks.example: If a triangle becomes a square, it may indicate an increase of one side.

tricks.title: Line Counting Trick
tricks.explanation: Counting lines or sides often helps in classification questions.
tricks.example: Three figures have 4 lines and one figure has 5 lines.

tricks.title: Identify Rotation
tricks.explanation: Observe the direction of arrows or symbols to identify rotation.
tricks.example: If an arrow changes from pointing upward to pointing right, it indicates a 90° clockwise rotation.

tricks.title: Check Inner and Outer Shapes
tricks.explanation: Observe whether the inner and outer shapes have been exchanged or changed.
tricks.example: A triangle inside a circle becomes a circle inside a triangle.

tricks.title: Observe Shading Pattern
tricks.explanation: Sometimes the shading pattern shifts position.
tricks.example: A black region may move from left to right.

tricks.title: Check Symmetry
tricks.explanation: In odd-one-out questions, symmetry may differ.
tricks.example: Three figures are symmetrical while one is not.

tricks.title: Dot Movement Trick
tricks.explanation: A dot may shift position in each step.
tricks.example: A dot moves from the top position to the right position.

tricks.title: Side Increase Rule
tricks.explanation: In polygon analogy, the number of sides may increase or decrease.
